classification.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-product rule to supplied factors and solve linear equations, recognising that a repeated factor gives one distinct root.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve equations are already factorised. The general factorisation skill accommodates the supplied non-monic linear factors in d, e and j.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates each factor of a zero product to zero, then solves the resulting linear equations. Repeated factors give one distinct solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-product rule to supplied factors, including linear factors with coefficients and repeated factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange where necessary, select factor pairs for monic quadratics, solve the factors and verify specified roots by substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Each part is a monic quadratic; c, e, f and l explicitly assess substitution checks as well as factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 moves all terms to the left, factorises, applies the zero-product rule and checks both roots by substituting into the original equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange and factorise monic quadratics, checking both solutions by substitution in four specified parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange and simplify coefficients before extracting a common variable factor, retaining the zero root rather than dividing it away.

questions.mappingNote: Every part reduces to a quadratic with a common variable factor and has zero as one solution.
questions.methodNote: Examples 2a and 3a factor out the variable after rearranging, simplifying a numerical common factor where useful. Example 3 warns against division by the variable because this loses the zero solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange where necessary and factor out the variable, retaining the zero solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose numerical simplification and rearrangement as needed, then use common-factor or monic factorisation and recognise a repeated root.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e use a common variable factor; f–o become monic quadratics after numerical simplification or rearrangement, including the repeated root in i.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 divides both sides by a nonzero numerical common factor, rearranges to zero, factorises and solves each factor equation. Division by a variable is avoided.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify numerical common factors and rearrange before solving common-factor or monic quadratic equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Select between difference-of-squares, repeated-factor and ordinary monic factorisation, with rearrangement or numerical simplification where needed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d and h–k use difference of squares; e–g and l–m use repeated factors; n–o require rearrangement and monic factorisation. The non-monic difference-of-squares items justify the general factorisation skill.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange to zero, simplify numerical common factors where useful, factorise and apply the null factor law. Example 4 explicitly demonstrates difference-of-squares equations; pages 2–3 establish factorisation and solving each linear factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply difference-of-squares or perfect-square factorisation, sometimes after numerical simplification or rearrangement.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a shared binomial, extract it to form a zero product and solve both factors, identifying coincident roots in part a.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts already contain repeated binomial factors, so common-binomial factorisation leads to the source's null factor law.
questions.methodNote: Factorise, then set each variable factor equal to zero; retain repeated roots once.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract a repeated binomial factor and apply the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose signed coefficient pairs with product ac and sum b, split and group the middle term, then solve the resulting linear factors.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the twelve parts is a non-monic quadratic already equal to zero; the displayed Example 5a reference directly matches the assessed method.
questions.methodNote: Example 5a: split the middle term into terms whose coefficients have product ac and sum b, group, factorise and apply the null factor law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Split the middle term and factorise non-monic quadratics, including fractional solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange to zero with correct signs, simplify a common numerical factor where useful, then select a middle-term split and solve the factors.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires rearrangement before non-monic factorisation; part l also permits division by 2. The printed reference is Example 5b.
questions.methodNote: Example 5b: move all terms to one side, split the middle term, factorise by grouping and set factors equal to zero. Divide out a numerical common factor where present.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange before splitting the middle term and solving non-monic quadratics.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise non-monic quadratics with signed coefficients and numerical common factors.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts assess factorisation of non-monic quadratics; c, d, f and j benefit from numerical division, and e from changing all signs. The variable a is retained in d–f.
questions.methodNote: Divide out numerical common factors, including negative factors, then split the middle term, factorise by grouping and apply the null factor law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise non-monic quadratics with signed coefficients and numerical common factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the supplied products, collect terms into a zero equation and choose monic or common-variable factorisation while preserving zero solutions.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts reduce to monic quadratics. Parts g and h reduce to quadratics with a common factor x, so division by x would incorrectly discard a solution. Page 6 supports factorisation and the null factor law; page 9 reinforces expansion and rearrangement before factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Expand, collect terms on one side, factorise and apply the null factor law. Example 6a on page 8 demonstrates this sequence and substitution checks.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand brackets and rearrange before factorising; two parts require retaining the zero solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify denominator restrictions and suitable multipliers, transform rational equations into polynomial equations, then factorise or recognise linear cancellation and check admissibility.

questions.mappingNote: Examples 6b and 7 supply denominator-clearing methods; Example 5 supplies non-monic factorisation. Parts a–h, j–n involve pronumeral denominators; i has numerical denominators. Part m simplifies to a linear equation after cancellation of equal quadratic terms.
questions.methodNote: Multiply by the common denominator, expand and rearrange, factorise using splitting and grouping where necessary, then apply the null factor law. Exclude zero denominators and check solutions in the original equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear numerical and algebraic denominators, rearrange and factorise; recognise excluded denominator values and the linear simplification in part m.

classification.difficultyReason: Move products to one side and extract their shared variable or binomial without cancelling possible roots, then simplify the remaining factor and solve.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies Example 8's shared-factor method. Parts a and c share x; parts b, d and e share a binomial. The general quadratic-factorisation skill covers all five parts, including the non-monic factors.
questions.methodNote: Example 8, Method 2: bring all terms to one side, extract the shared factor, simplify the remaining factor, and apply the null factor law. Do not divide by a factor that could be zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange equations with shared algebraic factors, factorise without cancelling possible zero factors, and apply the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange products and equations with algebraic denominators into monic or non-monic quadratics, then factorise and check valid roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d and i–l use denominator clearing before factorisation; e–h use product expansion and rearrangement. Parts g, h, k and l require non-monic factorisation, so solve-quadratic-factorisation is the most advanced directly assessed primary skill. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete twelve-part task.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 demonstrates splitting the middle term and grouping for non-monic quadratics. Example 6 expands and rearranges disguised quadratics. Example 7 clears algebraic denominators, factorises, applies the null factor law and checks solutions against the original equation. Examples 8 and 9 reinforce expansion, rearrangement and denominator clearing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange products and equations with algebraic denominators into monic or non-monic quadratics, then factorise and check valid roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate denominator restrictions, common-denominator multiplication and subtraction of expanded products, then recognise the resulting linear or quadratic form and validate roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c and d follow Example 9 directly; part b simplifies to a linear equation after applying its restriction. Part e uses non-monic factorisation by grouping, and part f uses the null factor law after extracting a common factor.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 clears denominators before expanding, collecting terms and factorising. Examples 6–8 support rearrangement, denominator restrictions, checking solutions and retaining zero solutions. Example 5 supports splitting the middle term for non-monic factorisation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear multiple denominators, expand and factorise the resulting equations while retaining denominator restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a whole-number product into a quadratic and reject the negative root.

questions.mappingNote: Example 10 on page 11 models a product of translated expressions and rejects a negative contextual root; the same method applies to the whole-number product.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral, model the product, rearrange, factorise, use the null factor law and interpret the roots in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a whole-number product into a quadratic and reject the negative root.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a product involving three less than an unknown and interpret both roots.

questions.mappingNote: The translated product follows Example 10; the whole-number domain excludes the negative root.
questions.methodNote: Model with a quadratic, factorise, apply the null factor law and reject roots outside the stated domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a product involving three less than an unknown and interpret both roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic from an integer product and recognise that both roots are allowed.

questions.mappingNote: Unlike the preceding whole-number questions, this integer task permits the negative root.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral, model the product and solve by factorisation, interpreting the stated domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic from an integer product and recognise that both roots are allowed.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an integer times twice itself into a quadratic, solve the difference of squares and recognise that both positive and negative integers satisfy the context.

questions.mappingNote: Page 4 demonstrates numerical-factor reduction and difference-of-squares equations; the application requires accepting both integer roots.
questions.methodNote: Model the product, divide by the numerical common factor and use a difference of squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate twice an integer into a simple square equation and retain both integer roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the hypotenuse from the right-angle diagram, form a Pythagorean equation with algebraic side lengths, solve the quadratic and reject geometrically invalid lengths.

questions.mappingNote: The right-angle marker identifies the sum-of-squares relationship. Quadratic solving is supported; original teaching evidence for that geometric prerequisite remains required.
questions.methodNote: The supplied pages teach rearrangement, numerical-factor reduction, factorisation and contextual root rejection. The required prerequisite Pythagorean modelling demonstration is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the right-angle relationship to form a quadratic, expand squared binomials and reject a geometrically invalid root.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the required sum, factor a non-monic quadratic by splitting the middle term and reject a fractional term count.

questions.mappingNote: Example 11 on page 12 demonstrates precisely this sequence-sum modelling method and contextual rejection of an inadmissible root.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the desired sum into the supplied formula, rearrange, split the middle term, factor by grouping and retain a positive whole-number term count.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the required sum, factor a non-monic quadratic by splitting the middle term and reject a fractional term count.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer that each base dimension loses twice the cut-out side length, model their product as the given area and reject a root that makes the box dimensions impossible.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed skill is quadratic modelling of the box base. Original prerequisite teaching for cut-out dimensions and rectangular area is missing.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 models a rectangle using a pronumeral, factorises the quadratic and rejects a contextually impossible length. Example 5 supports factorisation; Example 11 includes a contextual check.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model the reduced base dimensions and reject the geometrically impossible root.

classification.difficultyReason: Relate path area to outer area minus lawn area, increase both dimensions by twice the path width, then solve the quadratic and select a positive width.

questions.mappingNote: A quadratic models the surrounding path. Original prerequisite teaching for composite rectangular areas and uniform border dimensions is missing.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 models rectangular area, factorises and rejects a negative length; Example 11 checks the contextual result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the outer dimensions using twice the path width and compare the two areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a difference of journey times using reciprocal speeds and solve the resulting quadratic.

questions.mappingNote: The task combines reciprocal journey times with quadratic modelling. Original distance–time–speed teaching is missing.
questions.methodNote: Examples 7 and 9 clear algebraic denominators; Examples 10 and 11 solve contextual quadratics and reject unsuitable roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a difference of journey times using reciprocal speeds and solve the resulting quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert minutes to hours and model the time saving with reciprocal speeds.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed skill is quadratic word-problem modelling. Original speed–time and time-unit conversion teaching is missing.
questions.methodNote: Examples 7 and 9 clear denominators; Examples 10 and 11 interpret and check roots of contextual quadratics.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert minutes to hours and model the time saving with reciprocal speeds.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce the unknown speed and model the difference of two reciprocal journey times.

questions.mappingNote: The task models a time difference using speeds. Original distance–time–speed teaching is missing.
questions.methodNote: Examples 7 and 9 clear algebraic denominators. Examples 10 and 11 model a context and reject unsuitable roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Introduce the unknown speed and model the difference of two reciprocal journey times.

classification.difficultyReason: Express all individual times relative to the unknown joint time and reframe those times as additive reciprocal work rates before solving and interpreting the resulting quadratic.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires addition of reciprocal work rates before solving a quadratic. Original work-rate teaching is missing.
questions.methodNote: Examples 7 and 9 support clearing denominators; Examples 10 and 11 support contextual quadratic modelling and root selection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model three individual work rates in terms of the unknown joint completion time.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate each supplied quadratic over the stated interval, represent the values as a smooth parabola and identify its vertex from the minimum and symmetry.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is y=x²+c and directly assesses plotting a parabola and identifying its vertex. Example 12 on page 14 supplies the referenced method.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate y at integer x-values, plot the corresponding points and join them with a smooth curve. Example 12 identifies the vertex using the minimum y-value and symmetry about x=0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot six vertical translations of y=x² over a specified domain and identify their vertices.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires forming value tables, choosing suitable scales and plotting smooth curves within the domains. The hardest parts require recognising equal outputs and evaluating their midpoint to locate a vertex between integer inputs, using the taught symmetry method.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts require plotting from given equations over bounded domains. The table-to-graph skill is the closest primary match; identifying parabola features supports checking the plots.
questions.methodNote: Complete a table of values, plot the points and join them with a smooth curve. Use equal y-values to recognise symmetry; where necessary evaluate at the midpoint to locate the vertex, following Example 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate values and plot translated and vertically stretched parabolas over specified domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Links substitution, table construction and plotting downward-opening parabolas. Part c requires recognising symmetry between equal outputs at x=0 and x=1 and evaluating x=0.5 to capture the maximum, following the taught method.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess plotting a quadratic from values over a bounded domain. The table-based graphing skill is the closest catalogue match; technology is not required by this task.
questions.methodNote: Complete a table of values, plot the corresponding points and join them with a smooth curve. Use equal values to identify symmetry and locate the vertex, as in Examples 12 and 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct tables of values and plot four downward-opening parabolas over specified domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires plotting from values, locating the vertex using symmetry, and solving by factorisation. The final part explicitly asks students to connect algebraic roots with graph crossings by explaining that y=0 on the x-axis; preceding parts scaffold this routine connection.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses the taught table-and-plot method; part b uses monic factorisation; part c connects the equation y=0 with the graph's x-intercepts. The table-based graphing skill is the closest catalogue match; technology is not required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 teach forming a table of values, plotting the corresponding points and joining them with a smooth curve. Pages 2–3 teach factorisation followed by the null factor law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot a quadratic using values, solve its equation by factorisation and connect the solutions with the graph's x-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect a quadratic graph constructed from values with algebraic roots and their interpretation as x-intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses graphing from values; part b uses monic factorisation; part c connects zero values of y with the graph's x-intercepts. None of the supplied reuse candidates is the same whole task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 construct quadratic graphs using a table of values, plotted points and a smooth curve, with symmetry locating the vertex. Pages 2–3 teach factorisation followed by the null factor law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a quadratic graph constructed from values with algebraic roots and their interpretation as x-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate and plot values, solve the quadratic by factorisation, and explain why its roots are the graph's x-intercepts. The parts explicitly guide this routine connection between algebra and graph.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the table-and-plot method of Example 13. Part b uses monic factorisation as in Example 2. Part c links the zeros of the equation to the graph's x-intercepts.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 teach calculating a table of values, plotting its points and joining them with a smooth parabola. Pages 2–3 teach rearranging to zero, factorising and applying the null factor law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a quadratic plotted from values with algebraic solutions and the meaning of its x-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Take both square roots, isolate the pronumeral and simplify exact surds, including shifted squares and fractional constants.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f directly assess ax²=c; parts g–o apply the same square-root method to already completed squares. No expansion or fresh completion of the square is required.
questions.methodNote: Isolate the square, take both positive and negative square roots, then isolate x. Page 4 demonstrates rearranging to x²=c; pages 16–17 demonstrate exact surd and fractional roots after isolating a shifted square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Take both square roots, isolate the pronumeral and simplify exact surds, including shifted squares and fractional constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the specified completing-square method, isolate the square, retain both square roots and simplify surds where needed. These are routine linked algebraic steps with no method selection.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly requires completing the square; all linear coefficients are even. Solutions retain the add-and-subtract step and both roots, simplifying surds where possible.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 on page 16 adds and subtracts the square of half the linear coefficient, rewrites the perfect square, isolates it and takes both square roots. Pages 15–18 explain exact surd solutions and the same method with fractional coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square with even linear coefficients and simplify exact surd solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square using half the linear coefficient, then take both square roots and isolate x. Fractional square terms follow the taught procedure without introducing a new strategic decision.

questions.mappingNote: Every part explicitly requests completing the square. Odd coefficients require fractional square terms; f and g use integer square terms, while j and k finish with rational roots. All parts therefore map directly to complete-the-square-solve.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 begins on PDF page 16 and continues on page 17: add and subtract the square of half the linear coefficient, collect the constant, complete the square, take both square roots and isolate x. Example 16 confirms the same method for rational roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete squares with odd and even linear coefficients, retaining fractional intermediate values and exact surd solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square, including a fractional half-coefficient, and explain why a negative square value gives no real solution.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts explicitly require completing the square to establish the absence of real solutions. This directly assesses complete-the-square-solve rather than factorisation or the quadratic formula.
questions.methodNote: Add and subtract the square of half the coefficient of x, rewrite as a completed square, and isolate that square. Page 17 explicitly demonstrates that a real square cannot equal a negative number; pages 16–17 cover integer and fractional half-coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square, including a fractional half-coefficient, and explain why a negative square value gives no real solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Read h and k from vertex form to state the turning point and axis, handling opposite signs inside brackets and reordered constants.

questions.mappingNote: Each of a–i asks for these two features from an already completed-square expression, including reordered terms in h and i.
questions.methodNote: For y=(x-h)²+k, the turning point is (h,k) and the axis is x=h; Example 17 explicitly identifies h and k.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the turning point and symmetry axis directly from completed-square form.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught completing-square transformation by halving the linear coefficient, adding and subtracting its square, and collecting the constant. The required final form supplies the strategy.

questions.mappingNote: a–c use integer half-coefficients; d–f use fractional half-coefficients as in Example 18b. Every result is in the requested vertex form.
questions.methodNote: Example 18 adds and subtracts the square of half the coefficient of x, groups the perfect square and simplifies the constant.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square with even and odd linear coefficients, retaining exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve already completed-square equations using both square roots, exact surds and fractions, recognising when no real solution exists.

questions.mappingNote: a–c, e–g, i and k–n require square roots of an already isolated or readily isolated square, including exact fractional surds; d, h, j and o require the non-negativity argument.
questions.methodNote: Isolate the square, take both positive and negative square roots, then isolate x. The page 17 example explains that a negative square gives no real solution; pages 21–22 use this method for intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve already completed-square equations using both square roots, exact surds and fractions, recognising when no real solution exists.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the vertex, calculate intercepts by setting each coordinate to zero, and combine these features into a sketch. Interpret square equations to distinguish two crossings, tangency and no real intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part is already in vertex form, matching Example 19a,b directly. Fractional and surd coordinates require the same intercept method; no technology or table method is substituted.
questions.methodNote: Example 17 reads the turning point from y=(x-h)^2+k. Example 19a,b finds the y-intercept by x=0 and x-intercepts by y=0, solves the resulting square equation exactly, and sketches the upward parabola through these features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch translated monic parabolas from vertex form, including exact surd and fractional intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform expanded quadratics into vertex form, determine real intercepts and coordinate these results in a sketch. The student must organise the taught procedures and interpret whether the parabola crosses, touches or misses the x-axis.

questions.mappingNote: Every part a–o is an expanded monic quadratic matching Example 19c. Parts a, b, c, l and m have positive minima; e has a repeated root; d, f, g, h, i, j, k, n and o have two real roots. Half-integer vertices and exact surd intercepts follow the inspected completing-square and square-root demonstrations.
questions.methodNote: Examples 18 and 19 complete the square to obtain the vertex, substitute x=0 for the y-intercept, and solve y=0 by square roots for the x-intercepts before sketching an upward parabola.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square and find exact intercepts, including surds and half-integer vertices, before sketching.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the null factor law to supplied linear factors, including factors with non-unit coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess solving already-factorised quadratics; parts d–f include non-unit linear coefficients, so the general factorisation skill is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Use the null factor law, equate each supplied factor to zero and solve the resulting linear equations, as demonstrated in Example 1 on PDF page 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the null factor law to supplied linear factors, including factors with non-unit coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise factorisation as suitable, select signed factor pairs matching the constant and linear coefficient, and apply the null factor law to obtain both roots. All equations are already monic and equal to zero.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is a monic quadratic already equal to zero, matching the factorisation method demonstrated in Example 2.
questions.methodNote: Factorise the quadratic expression, equate each factor to zero using the null factor law, and solve the resulting linear equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Monic quadratics are already equal to zero and require integer factorisation followed by the null factor law.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and apply common-factor, perfect-square, difference-of-squares and non-monic factorisation methods, including rearrangement and fractional roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and e use repeated factors; b and i use difference of squares; c uses a common algebraic factor; d first divides by 3; f and g use non-monic factorisation; h uses division and square roots. The most advanced assessed method is non-monic quadratic factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange to zero, divide out a numerical common factor where useful, factorise and apply the null factor law. Page 6 Example 5 explicitly teaches splitting the middle term and grouping for non-monic quadratics; page 4 also permits direct square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and apply common-factor, perfect-square, difference-of-squares and non-monic factorisation methods, including rearrangement and fractional roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines direct square-root equations with completing the square, including odd linear coefficients and exact surd solutions.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed method is completing the square in d–f; a–c assess solving equations by isolating a square.
questions.methodNote: For a–c, isolate the squared expression and take both square roots. For d–f, complete the square and take both square roots, retaining exact surds. Pages 16–17 demonstrate completing the square with even and odd linear coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines direct square-root equations with completing the square, including odd linear coefficients and exact surd solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose values within each specified domain, calculate coordinates and translate them into a smooth parabola with appropriate scales and endpoints. This links familiar substitution and plotting procedures; the four repetitions add no new demand.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 5a–d explicitly asks for plotting over a finite interval, matching the table-and-plot method of Examples 12–13. The graph-from-tables skill is the closest catalogue match; technology is not required by this source question.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 Examples 12–13 teach making a table of values, plotting points and joining them with a smooth parabola over a specified domain. Pages 20–22 support vertex and intercept identification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate quadratic values and plot smooth parabolas over four specified finite domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear numerical or algebraic denominators, rearrange and factorise where required, retaining denominator restrictions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a clears a numerical denominator and uses non-monic factorisation as in Example 5. Part b is linear as printed and is solved by clearing numerical denominators. Part c uses Example 9's common-denominator method, followed by non-monic factorisation and substitution checks.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange to zero, factorise and use the null factor law. Examples 6–9 clear denominators before rearranging; pages 8–9 state denominator restrictions and checking in the original equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear numerical or algebraic denominators, rearrange and factorise where required, retaining denominator restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete squares with even and odd linear coefficients and express irrational solutions exactly.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts explicitly assess solving by completing the square. Parts a–c follow Example 14; parts d–f follow Example 15. The supplied reuse candidates have different mathematical tasks and are ineligible.
questions.methodNote: Add and subtract the square of half the linear coefficient, collect the constant, isolate the completed square, then take both square roots and isolate x. Example 14 supports even coefficients; Example 15 supports fractional halves.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete squares with even and odd linear coefficients and express irrational solutions exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Select factorisation or completing the square; later parts require exact surd solutions and fractional square completion.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e and g factorise over the integers. Parts f and h–l require the square-completion method, retaining exact surds. Solving by completing the square is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 uses factorisation and the null factor law. Example 14 completes the square for even linear coefficients; Example 15 completes the square with fractional terms for odd coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select factorisation or completing the square; later parts require exact surd solutions and fractional square completion.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify excluded denominator values, choose a common denominator, rearrange the resulting equation and factorise a non-monic quadratic before checking admissibility. These are several linked but explicitly taught procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 9a–d becomes a factorisable quadratic after clearing denominators. Non-monic factorisation is directly assessed in b–d, so solve-quadratic-factorisation is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–10 teach nonzero-denominator restrictions, multiplication by a common denominator or cross-multiplication, rearrangement to a quadratic, factorisation and checking solutions.
